name: The Achaemenid Empire
title: Social Hierarchy of the Achaemenid Empire: From King of Kings to Slave
in: the Persian Empire of Darius I
period: 550–330 BCE (from Cyrus the Great to Darius III)

tiers.name: The King of Kings
tiers.you: You rule “by the grace of Ahuramazda” over lands of every people, whose envoys bring you gifts and whose satraps send you tribute, but even a king can be murdered in his bed.
tiers.kid: The King of Kings ruled a huge empire, and people from many lands brought him gifts.
tiers.rise: The throne stayed in the Achaemenid family and usually went to a son of the king, but rivals fought for it: Darius I claimed descent from a side branch of the family, and Artaxerxes II had to defeat his brother Cyrus the Younger at Cunaxa in 401 BCE.
tiers.why: The Great King was, in the words of Darius I’s tomb, “King of Kings, King of countries containing all kinds of men”, and he ruled, as Darius proclaimed at Behistun, “by the grace of Ahuramazda”.

tiers.name: Royal kin and the great houses
tiers.you: You belong to one of the great Persian houses: your kinsmen govern satrapies and command armies, your sisters may marry into the king’s family, and a single act of disloyalty could destroy your whole house.
tiers.kid: Noble Persian families helped the king rule, leading his armies and governing his provinces.
tiers.rise: Birth and marriage decided who belonged, and the king tied the great houses to the throne by marrying their daughters and giving them his own; a noble who lost his trust could lose his life and his family.
tiers.why: Below the king stood his own clan, the Achaemenids, and a small circle of great Persian houses.

tiers.name: Satraps and high officials
tiers.you: You govern a province for the King of Kings from a court of your own, collecting his tribute and judging its cases, but your secretary and treasurer answer to him directly, and his displeasure can cost you your life.
tiers.kid: Satraps governed the empire’s provinces for the king, collecting taxes and keeping the roads safe.
tiers.rise: The king appointed satraps, mostly from the Persian nobility, and could recall or execute them; lower offices were open to men of many peoples who could serve him, from the Elamite and Babylonian scribes of the treasuries to Egyptian and Jewish courtiers.
tiers.why: A satrap (xšaçapāvan, “protector of the province”) governed each of the empire’s 20 to 30 provinces with an almost royal court of his own.

tiers.name: Magi
tiers.you: You are a magus: no Persian offering is made without you, and you sing the hymns at the sacrifice, interpret dreams and draw rations from the royal stores for the gods’ offerings.
tiers.kid: Magi were Persian priests who led prayers and offerings to the gods.
tiers.rise: Magi were born into their priestly tribe; the most trusted served at court, where, Greek writers say, they interpreted the king’s dreams and helped to educate royal princes.
tiers.why: The magi were the priests of the Persians and Medes.

tiers.name: Persian warriors
tiers.you: You are a Persian of the homeland, taught as a boy to ride, shoot the bow and speak the truth; your land pays no tribute, but when the king calls up the army you march, and if you are among the best you serve in the Immortals.
tiers.kid: Persian men formed the heart of the king’s army, and the Greeks called his best troops the Immortals.
tiers.rise: Persian birth made a man one of the ruling people; service in the king’s wars could bring gifts and promotion, and Darius I himself, according to Herodotus, had served Cambyses II as a spear-bearer before he seized the throne.
tiers.why: The Persians of Persis (Pārsa), in south-western Iran, were the ruling people of the empire, and in Old Persian one word, kāra, meant both “people” and “army”.

tiers.name: Tribute-paying subjects
tiers.you: You farm or work at a trade in one of the subject lands, under your own laws and gods; each year your satrapy sends the king its tribute, and you may be called to serve in his army or on his building works.
tiers.kid: Most people in the empire were farmers and craftspeople from many lands, who paid taxes to the king.
tiers.rise: Service to the king, as soldier, scribe or courtier, could lift a subject; rebellion brought the opposite, and Herodotus describes the people of rebel cities, such as Barca and Miletus, enslaved or deported.
tiers.why: Most of the empire’s people, farmers, herders, craftsmen and townspeople, lived in its subject lands, the dahyāva, from Egypt and Ionia to Babylonia, Bactria and the Indus; the Behistun inscription lists twenty-three…

tiers.name: Workers on rations (kurtaš)
tiers.you: You work on the king’s buildings or estates near Persepolis and draw a monthly ration of grain and wine from his storehouses; if you are a skilled craftswoman, you are paid as much as the men.
tiers.kid: Workers from many lands built the palaces of Persepolis and were paid in food such as grain and wine.
tiers.rise: Some kurtaš were deportees brought in to work on the royal building projects; skill and the leadership of a work group brought higher rations.
tiers.why: The Persepolis Fortification tablets, written in Elamite between 509 and 493 BCE, record the rations that the royal administration of the homeland issued each month to its workers, the kurtaš.

tiers.name: Slaves
tiers.you: You are owned by a Babylonian household or a Persian noble’s estate, which can sell you by a registered and taxed contract; if your owner allows, you may run a business of your own and pay a fixed sum to your master.
tiers.kid: Slaves were owned by other people and had to work without pay; many were captives taken in war.
tiers.rise: Owners could free slaves by a written deed, often on condition that the freed person support them for the rest of their lives; children born to slave women were slaves.
tiers.why: Slavery was an old institution in Babylonia, Egypt and Media, and it continued under Persian rule.
